blocks.text: [III, 375] Of this there are two kinds: one domestic, from bees that are kept at home; the other wild, such as John is said to have lived on in the desert, Matth. III, 4. His food was locusts and wild honey. And Marc. I, 6. Eating locusts and wild honey. Since the two Evangelists expressly write μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion], wild honey, it is surprising that there are some who understand μελαγρίαν [melagrian] as a kind of plant which, if we believe them, grows in the desert. Suidas: Μελαγρία· εἶδος βοτάνης φυομένης ἐν ἐρήμῳ [Melagria; eidos botanēs phyomenēs en erēmō]. Others write τὰ μέλαγρα [ta melagra], as though there were a plant of this name, which they otherwise call ἀκρίδας [akridas]. Theophylact: Τινὲς λέγουσι βοτάνας εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας, ἃς καὶ μέλαγρα καλοῦσι [Tines legousi botanas einai tas akridas, has kai melagra kalousi]; Some say that the acrides are plants, which they also call melagra. Even if we granted this, it would still be beside the point. For we do not read that John ate μελαγρίαν [melagrian] or μέλαγρα [melagra], but μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion]. No more acceptable is what Bede in his book De locis sanctis, and Thomas on Matthew, report from Arnulphus or Archulphus: that in the desert of John there were trees with broad, round leaves, of milky colour and honeyed taste, which, being naturally brittle, are rubbed in the hands and eaten, and that this is called wild honey. [col. 519] Nor do I agree with Christianus Druthmarus, for whom the wild honey in this passage is that very Manna on which the children of Israel were fed for forty years. The taste of Manna was indeed כצפיחת בדבש, like the taste of a honeyed wafer, Exod. XVI, 31. And accordingly Manna is called by some δροσόμελι [drosomeli] and ἀερόμελι [aeromeli] ^{(3)}. Yet Manna is one thing, wild [III, 376] honey another. Nor should new meanings be foisted onto the words of Scripture when the received ones can fit. Here, therefore, I understand nothing other than locusts and wild honey. And we have already shown ^{a)} that locusts are frequent in those regions and therefore were accepted as food. The same about wild honey is easy to prove from Scripture itself. Well known is the saying of Solomon, Prov. XXV, 16: Have you found honey? Eat as much as is sufficient. And this doubtless refers to wild honey, which was found here and there in the fields. Thus when Samson had come upon a lion in the field and torn it apart, [III, 377] in the following year he found honey which bees had produced in its carcass, Iud. XIV, 8. Of the same kind is what we read in 1 Sam. XIV, 25. 26: The people came into the forest, in which there was honey על פני השדה, on the surface of the field. And the people entered that forest, and behold הלך דבש, a flow of honey. This, namely, was wild honey, which bees had made either on the bare ground, or in hollow trees, or in clefts of rocks. Such a rock is called in Hebrew צור דבש, rock of honey, Ps. LXXXI, 17. And the honey flowing from it is דבש מסלע, honey from the rock, Deut. XXXII, 13. So from the word יער jaar, which means forest (as jar in Punic means wood according to Augustine on Psalm 23), יער jaar, or יערה jaara, is a honeycomb, properly one found in the forest. As in 1 Sam. XIV, 27: Jonathan stretched out the tip of the rod that he had in his hand, and dipped it ביערת הדבש, in the honeycomb. And Cant. V, 1: I have eaten יערי, my honeycomb with my honey ^{(4)}. Nor is there reason for anyone to believe that it was peculiar to Judaea that bees made honey here and there in fields or forests. For we have already learned ^{b)} the same of Scythia and Muscovy from reliable writers. And Maldonatus on Matthew reports that he saw poor men in Baetica who gathered honey from the forests and made their living by selling it. Accordingly the poets frequently mention bees [III, 378] that nest in hollow trees, in reed-beds, or in caves. Hesiod, Theogony, line 230:
— — — οὔρεσι δὲ δρῦς Ἄκρη μέν τε φέρει βαλάνους, μέσση δὲ μελίσσας, [ouresi de drys / akrē men te pherei balanous, messē de melissas,]

On the mountains the oak bears acorns at its top, and bees in its middle. That is, ἐν τοῖς κοιλώμασι τῶν στελέχων [en tois koilōmasi tōn stelechōn], in the hollows of the trunks, as the Scholiast there explains. Phocylides, or whoever he is, in the Νουθετικῷ [Nouthetikō], line 160:

Κάμνει δ' ἠερόφοιτος, ἀριστοπόνος τε μέλισσα, Ἠὲ πέτρης κοίλης κατὰ χηραμὸν, ἢ δονάκεσσιν, Ἢ δρυὸς ὠγυγίης κατὰ κοιλάδος· [Kamnei d' ēerophoitos, aristoponos te melissa, / Ēe petrēs koilēs kata chēramon, ē donakessin, / Ē dryos ōgygiēs kata koilados;]
The air-roaming and hard-working bee also labours, either in the cave of a hollow rock, or among reeds, or in the hollow of an ancient oak. Virgil, Georgics, book 4 [vv. 43 ff.]:
Often too (if the report is true) they have made their home in hollows dug beneath the earth, and have been found deep within porous rocks and in the cavity of a hollowed tree.
So when a shepherd, about to plunder, has driven the armed bees from their pumice cave. — — —
— — and, sent forth from the hollow belly of a beech, the honey-bearing army hums over the chosen herbs.
